tips.title: Brackets round every value you put in
tips.body: Write $x = -3$ in as $(-3)$ every time. It keeps the minus sign attached to its number, it makes $(-3)^2 = 9$ come out right, and it tells a calculator what you mean: $-3^2$ typed without brackets gives $-9$.

tips.title: The power is on the letter, not the number in front
tips.body: $2x^2$ squares only the $x$. With $x = 3$ that is $2 \times 9 = 18$. Squaring $2 \times 3$ gives 36, which is $(2x)^2$, a different expression. The same goes for $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$: square the $v$ and nothing else.

tips.title: Substitute first, then solve
tips.body: If the letter you want is not on its own, you do not need to rearrange the formula. Put in every value you know, and what is left is an ordinary equation: in $v = u + at$ with $v = 26$, $u = 8$ and $t = 6$, that is $26 = 8 + 6a$, so $a = 3$.

tips.title: Estimate before you press equals
tips.body: A rough answer in your head catches a missed bracket. For $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 1200 \times 13^2$, $13^2$ is about 170 and half of 1200 is 600, so expect about 100 000. An answer near a million or near a thousand means a typing slip.

tips.title: Keep the full value, and round once at the end
tips.body: Use the calculator's full answer, or its answer memory, all the way through. Rounding $r^3 = 17.576$ to $17.6$ part-way through $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ turns $73.6$ into $73.7$.

why.matters:
A formula is a calculation written once, with letters where the numbers go, so that anyone can do it again for their own numbers. Substitution is the other half of that bargain: putting this time's numbers in place of the letters.

Almost every formula you will ever use is used this way, in science, in finance, in a spreadsheet, and the mistakes are always the same few: a negative value without its bracket, a power applied to too much, a rounded number carried forward. Getting substitution reliable is what makes every formula after it usable.

examples.title: The temperature where both scales agree
examples.body:
Weather apps in the UK give Celsius, and in the US Fahrenheit. The formula between them is $F = 1.8C + 32$. At 0 °C water freezes, and $F = 1.8(0) + 32 = 32$ °F. At 100 °C it boils, and $F = 180 + 32 = 212$ °F. Body temperature, 37 °C, is $66.6 + 32 = 98.6$ °F.

Now substitute a negative: $C = -40$ gives $F = 1.8(-40) + 32 = -72 + 32 = -40$. At minus 40 the two scales read the same number, the one temperature where it does not matter which thermometer you own. The bracket round $-40$ is what gets you there.

props.title: F = 1.8C + 32, one row at a time

visual.alt: A table converting Celsius to Fahrenheit: minus 40 gives minus 40, 0 gives 32, 37 gives 98.6, and 100 gives 212

examples.title: Body mass index
examples.body:
Doctors use body mass index, $\text{BMI} = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{height}^2}$, with mass in kilograms and height in metres. For someone of 70 kg and 1.75 m, the height is squared first: $1.75^2 = 3.0625$, and $70 \div 3.0625 = 22.9$ to 1 decimal place.

Divide by the height only once and you get 40.0. Double the height instead of squaring it and you get 20. Both are plausible-looking numbers, which is exactly why the power has to be read as written, on the height and nothing else: the formula does not warn you when it has been misread.

props.title: The same numbers, three readings of one formula

visual.alt: A table of three ways to work out BMI for 70 kilograms and 1.75 metres: squaring the height gives 22.9, which is right; not squaring gives 40.0 and doubling gives 20.0, both wrong

examples.title: A spreadsheet column
examples.body:
In a spreadsheet, a cell holding $=\text{B2}*\text{C2}$ is a formula whose letters are cell names. Copy it down the column and the spreadsheet substitutes each row's own numbers: price times quantity for every line of an order.

That is substitution done a thousand times without a slip, and it goes wrong in the same ways as by hand. A formula that needs a bracket and lacks one is wrong on every row at once.

props.title: One formula, each row substituting its own values

visual.alt: A spreadsheet order: row 2 has price 1 pound 20 and quantity 5, giving 6 pounds; row 3 has 85p and 12, giving 10 pounds 20; row 4 has 4 pounds 50 and 3, giving 13 pounds 50

steps.title: Letters stand for numbers
steps.body:
**To substitute is to replace each letter with its value, then work the calculation out.** A formula is a calculation written once so it can be used again with different numbers, and substitution is how it gets used.

The perimeter of a rectangle is $P = 2l + 2w$. For a rectangle 7 cm long and 4 cm wide, $l = 7$ and $w = 4$:

$$P = 2(7) + 2(4) = 14 + 8 = 22 \text{ cm}$$

**Three habits make it reliable:**

- **Write each value in brackets** as you put it in. It costs nothing with $7$, and it saves you with $-2$.
- **Letters written together multiply.** $3a$ means $3 \times a$, and $ab$ means $a \times b$. So with $a = 5$, $3a$ is $15$, not $35$.
- **Then follow the order of operations**: brackets, powers, multiplying and dividing, then adding and subtracting.

An **expression** such as $4a - 3b$ has no equals sign, and substituting gives its value. A **formula** such as $P = 2l + 2w$ says how one quantity, $P$, is worked out from others. You substitute into both in exactly the same way.

props.title: a = 5 and b = −2, each written in brackets first

visuals.alt: A table substituting a equals 5 and b equals minus 2: 4a is 20, ab is minus 10, 3b is minus 6, a minus b is 7, and 4a minus 3b is 26

check.prompt: Work out the value of $5p + 2q$ when $p = 3$ and $q = -4$.
check.solution: $5(3) + 2(-4) = 15 - 8 = 7$. Writing $(-4)$ in brackets keeps the minus attached to the 4.

steps.title: Powers come before multiplying
steps.body:
**A power belongs only to what it is written on.** In $2x^2$ the square is on the $x$, not on the $2x$. So with $x = 3$:

$$2x^2 = 2 \times 3^2 = 2 \times 9 = 18$$

Squaring first is the order of operations at work: **powers come before multiplying**. Working out $2 \times 3 = 6$ and then squaring gives $36$, which is the value of a different expression, $(2x)^2$.

**Negative values need their brackets most of all.** With $x = -4$, $x^2$ is $(-4)^2 = (-4) \times (-4) = 16$. Typed into a calculator as $-4^2$, without the brackets, it gives $-16$, because the calculator squares the 4 and then applies the minus. The bracket you wrote on paper is the one to type.

**And $-x^2$ is not the same as $(-x)^2$.** $-x^2$ means *square $x$, then make it negative*, so it is negative for every $x$ except 0, where it is 0: with $x = -4$ it is $-16$.

props.title: The power is on the x alone, unless a bracket says otherwise

visuals.alt: A table of values at x equals 3 and x equals minus 4: x squared is 9 and 16, 2x squared is 18 and 32, 2x all squared is 36 and 64, minus x squared is minus 9 and minus 16, x cubed is 27 and minus 64

check.prompt: Work out the value of $3x^2$ when $x = 4$.
check.solution: Square first: $4^2 = 16$, then $3 \times 16 = 48$. $144$ comes from squaring $3 \times 4$, which is $(3x)^2$; $24$ doubles the 12 instead of squaring the 4.

steps.title: Negative values: the brackets do the work
steps.body:
**Put the negative value in brackets, then let the sign rules do their job**: a negative times a negative is positive, and a negative squared is positive.

The commonest slip is in a term like $-5x$. With $x = -3$ it is $-5 \times (-3) = +15$, and dropping either minus sign turns it into $-15$.

steps.note: take the product with its sign, then subtract it

check.prompt: Work out the value of $x^2 - 4x$ when $x = -2$.
check.solution: $(-2)^2 - 4(-2) = 4 + 8 = 12$. Both terms come out positive: a negative squared, and a negative times a negative.

steps.title: Fraction bars and roots group what they cover
steps.body:
**A fraction bar works like a pair of brackets round the top and another round the bottom.** In $\dfrac{a + b}{c}$ you add first and divide after: with $a = 7$, $b = 5$, $c = 4$ it is $\dfrac{12}{4} = 3$, not $7 + \dfrac{5}{4}$.

**A root sign covers everything under it.** $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ with $a = 6$, $b = 8$ is $\sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10$, not $6 + 8$.

**On a calculator, type the brackets the bar and the root imply**: $(7 + 5) \div 4$, and $\sqrt{(36 + 64)}$. A calculator only knows about the grouping you give it.

visuals.problem: Work out $T = \dfrac{3m + n}{m - n}$ when $m = 4$ and $n = -1$.

steps.note: work out the whole numerator first
only now does the fraction bar act

check.prompt: Work out the value of $\sqrt{p^2 - q^2}$ when $p = 13$ and $q = 5$.
check.solution: Everything under the root first: $13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$, then $\sqrt{144} = 12$.

steps.title: Formulae from science
steps.body:
**The specification names scientific formulae**, and exam papers use them because they are real: $v = u + at$, $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. You are not expected to know the physics. The formula is given, the values are given, and the skill is the same substitution.

**Two things are new.** The letters can be subscripted, as in $E_k$, which is simply a name. And the values come with **units**: if every value is in the standard unit (metres, seconds, kilograms), the answer is in the standard unit too.

In $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ the square is on the $v$ only, as in the step on powers. With $m = 4$ kg and $v = 3$ m/s:

$$E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 3^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 9 = 18 \text{ J}$$

Squaring $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 3 = 6$ instead gives $36$, twice the right answer.

steps.title: When the letter you want is not the subject
steps.body:
**Sometimes the value you are given is the answer, and a letter on the right is the unknown.** You are told $v$, $u$ and $t$ and asked for $a$.

**Substitute everything you know, then solve the equation that is left.** There is no need to rearrange the formula first: once the numbers are in, it is an ordinary linear equation with one letter.

steps.note: three of the four letters are now numbers
put the answer back into the original

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Work out $4a + b$ when $a = 6$ and $b = -5$.
2. Work out $3x^2$ when $x = 2$.
3. $v = u + at$. Work out $v$ when $u = 20$, $a = -4$ and $t = 3$.

**Part B.**

4. Work out $x^2 + 2x$ when $x = -4$.
5. $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. Work out $E_k$ when $m = 10$ and $v = 3$.
6. Work out $\dfrac{a - b}{a + 2b}$ when $a = 5$ and $b = -1$.

**Part C.**

7. $v = u + at$. Find $t$ when $v = 30$, $u = 6$ and $a = 4$.
8. Work out $-x^2$ when $x = -5$, and explain why the answer is negative.
9. A student works out $3x^2$ when $x = -2$ and gets $36$. Find the mistake.

Write every value in brackets as you substitute, and do the powers before anything else.

steps.title: Going deeper: substitution as a test
steps.body:
**One value can prove a claim false.** The expression $n^2 + n + 41$ gives a prime number for every whole number $n$ from 0 to 39: 41, 43, 47, and on up to 1601. It looks like a rule. Substitute $n = 40$:

$$40^2 + 40 + 41 = 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41 \times 41$$

which is not prime. A single **counterexample** is enough to disprove *always*, and substitution is how you find one.

**No number of examples proves *always*.** Forty values that work say nothing about the forty-first. That is why proofs use algebra rather than substitution, and why a question that says *show that ... for all values* wants algebra.

**Keep the full value until the end.** The volume of a sphere is $V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$. With $r = 2.6$, $r^3 = 17.576$ and $V = 73.62\ldots$, which is $73.6$ to 1 decimal place. Rounding $r^3$ to $17.6$ first gives $73.72\ldots$, which is $73.7$: the early rounding has moved the final answer. Use the calculator's full value, or its answer memory, and round once, at the end.

props.title: Every value up to 39 works, and one value is enough to break it

visuals.alt: A table of n squared plus n plus 41: 43, 47 and 1601 are prime, but at n equals 40 the value is 1681, which is 41 times 41

check.prompt: A student claims that $n^2 - n + 11$ is prime for every whole number $n$. Which value of $n$ shows that the claim is false?
check.solution: At $n = 11$: $11^2 - 11 + 11 = 121 = 11 \times 11$, which is not prime. The other values give 31, 101 and 23, which are all prime, so they fit the claim without testing it.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- To **substitute**, replace each letter with its value and work the calculation out.
- **Write every value in brackets**, especially a negative one: $x = -3$ goes in as $(-3)$.
- **Letters written together multiply**: $3a$ is $3 \times a$, and $ab$ is $a \times b$.
- Follow the **order of operations**: brackets, powers, multiplying and dividing, adding and subtracting.
- A **power belongs to what it is written on**: $2x^2$ squares the $x$ only, so with $x = 3$ it is 18, not 36.
- **A negative squared is positive**: $(-4)^2 = 16$. But $-x^2$ is always negative or zero.
- A **fraction bar** groups the top and the bottom, and a **root** covers everything under it.
- **Scientific formulae** work the same way. Standard units in give standard units out.
- If the unknown letter is **not the subject**, substitute everything you know, then solve.
- **One counterexample disproves a claim**, but no number of examples proves one.
- **Round once, at the end**: rounding part-way through can change the answer.

rows: replace each letter with its value
18: the power is on the x
work out the top and bottom first
one value that breaks a claim

visuals.alt: A summary table of the rules: brackets round negative values, powers first, fraction bars group, substitute then solve, one counterexample disproves, and round at the end

check.prompt: Work out the value of $a - 2b$ when $a = 3$ and $b = -4$.
check.solution: $3 - 2(-4) = 3 + 8 = 11$. Subtracting a negative adds; $-5$ comes from treating $-2(-4)$ as $-8$.

questions.prompt: Work out the value of $3a + 2b$ when $a = 4$ and $b = 5$.
The perimeter of a rectangle is $P = 2l + 2w$. Work out $P$ when $l = 8.5$ cm and $w = 3$ cm.
Work out the value of $5x - y$ when $x = 3$ and $y = -4$.
questions.solution: $5(3) - (-4) = 15 + 4 = 19$. Subtracting a negative adds.

questions.prompt: Work out the value of $2x^2$ when $x = 5$.
questions.solution: Square first: $5^2 = 25$, then $2 \times 25 = 50$. $100$ is $(2 \times 5)^2$, which squares the 2 as well, and $20$ doubles the 5 twice.

questions.prompt: $v = u + at$. Work out $v$ when $u = 12$, $a = -3$ and $t = 2$.
Work out the value of $x^2 - 3x$ when $x = -5$.
questions.solution: $(-5)^2 - 3(-5) = 25 + 15 = 40$. A negative squared is positive, and $-3 \times -5$ is $+15$.

questions.prompt: $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. Work out $E_k$ when $m = 6$ and $v = 4$.
questions.solution: $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 4^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 16 = 48$. The square is on the $v$ alone.

questions.prompt: Work out the value of $\dfrac{a + 3b}{a - b}$ when $a = 7$ and $b = -1$.
$s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. Work out $s$ when $u = 5$, $t = 4$ and $a = -2$.
$v = u + at$. Find $a$ when $v = 35$, $u = 11$ and $t = 8$.
questions.solution: Substitute: $35 = 11 + 8a$. Subtract 11: $24 = 8a$. Divide by 8: $a = 3$. Check: $11 + 3 \times 8 = 35$ ✓.

questions.prompt: $y = -x^2$. What is the value of $y$ when $x = -3$?
questions.solution: $-x^2$ means square $x$, then make it negative: $(-3)^2 = 9$, so $y = -9$. Getting 9 squares the minus sign as well, which is $(-x)^2$.

questions.prompt: The area of a trapezium is $A = \tfrac{1}{2}(a + b)h$. A trapezium has parallel sides $a = 5$ cm and $b = 9$ cm, and an area of 42 cm². Find its height $h$.
questions.solution: Substitute: $42 = \tfrac{1}{2}(5 + 9)h = 7h$. Divide by 7: $h = 6$ cm.

questions.prompt: Amir works out $2x^2$ when $x = -3$ and gets $-18$. Beth works it out and gets $36$. Who is right?
questions.solution: **Neither of them: it is 18.** The square is on the $x$ alone, so $(-3)^2 = 9$ comes first, and then $2 \times 9 = 18$. Amir squared the 3 and kept the minus, which is $-2 \times 3^2$. Beth squared the whole of $2x$, which is $(2x)^2$.
options: Beth: the 2 and the −3 multiply to −6 first, and (−6)² is 36
Amir: the minus sign in x = −3 stays in front of the answer
Neither of them: it is 18, since (−3)² = 9 and 2 × 9 = 18
Both of them: it depends on the calculator being used

questions.prompt: A polygon with $n$ sides has $d = \dfrac{n(n - 3)}{2}$ diagonals. A polygon has 35 diagonals. How many sides does it have?
questions.solution: Substitute: $35 = \dfrac{n(n - 3)}{2}$, so $n(n - 3) = 70$. That is $n^2 - 3n - 70 = 0$, which factorises as $(n - 10)(n + 7) = 0$. A polygon cannot have $-7$ sides, so $n = 10$. Check: $\dfrac{10 \times 7}{2} = 35$ ✓.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown upwards from a height of 2 m. Its height in metres after $t$ seconds is $h = 2 + 14t - 5t^2$. After how many seconds is it back at a height of 2 m?
questions.solution: Substitute $h = 2$: $2 = 2 + 14t - 5t^2$, so $14t - 5t^2 = 0$. Factorise: $t(14 - 5t) = 0$, so $t = 0$ or $t = 2.8$. At $t = 0$ the ball is just being thrown, so it is back at 2 m after $2.8$ seconds.

questions.prompt: Nadia says that $n^2 + n + 17$ is a prime number for every whole number $n$. Which value of $n$ shows that she is wrong?
questions.solution: At $n = 16$: $16^2 + 16 + 17 = 256 + 33 = 289 = 17 \times 17$, which is not prime. The other values give 173, 127 and 257, which are prime, so they fit the claim without testing it.

questions.prompt: The time in seconds for one complete swing of a pendulum, there and back, is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$, where $l$ is its length in metres and $g = 9.8$. A clock needs a pendulum with $T = 2$. How long should the pendulum be? Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
questions.solution: Substitute: $2 = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{9.8}}$. Divide by $2\pi$: $\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{9.8}} = \dfrac{1}{\pi}$. Square both sides: $\dfrac{l}{9.8} = \dfrac{1}{\pi^2}$, so $l = \dfrac{9.8}{\pi^2} = 0.9929\ldots$, which is $0.99$ m to 2 decimal places.

questions.prompt: Sam and Tia work out $V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ with $r = 2.6$, to 1 decimal place. Sam rounds $r^3$ to $17.6$ first and gets $73.7$. Tia keeps every digit and gets $73.6$. Who is right?
questions.solution: **Tia is right.** $r^3 = 17.576$, and $\tfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 17.576 = 73.62\ldots$, which is $73.6$. Rounding to $17.6$ first gives $73.72\ldots$ Rounding part-way through changed the final answer, so keep the full value and round once, at the end. Using 3.14 would make the answer less exact, not more.

markScheme.description: Tia: early rounding changes the answer

options: Sam: rounding r³ first makes the working clearer to follow
Tia: rounding r³ part-way through moved the final answer
Sam: his answer is larger, so it is the safer one to give
Neither: π should have been taken as 3.14 to be exact

questions.prompt: A car starts from rest, so $u = 0$, and travels 100 m in 8 seconds with a constant acceleration $a$. Using $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$, find $a$.
questions.solution: Substitute: $100 = 0 \times 8 + \tfrac{1}{2}a \times 8^2 = 32a$. Divide by 32: $a = 3.125$ m/s².

questions.prompt:
The kinetic energy of a moving object is $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, with $m$ in kilograms, $v$ in m/s and $E_k$ in joules.

(a) Work out the kinetic energy of a car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 13 m/s.

(b) The car speeds up to 26 m/s. A student says that because the speed has doubled, the kinetic energy has doubled too. Use the formula to evaluate this claim.
questions.solution:
(a) $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1200 \times 13^2 = 600 \times 169 = 101\,400$ J.

(b) At 26 m/s, $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1200 \times 26^2 = 600 \times 676 = 405\,600$ J. That is $405\,600 \div 101\,400 = 4$ times as much, not twice. The student is wrong: the speed is squared in the formula, so doubling it multiplies the energy by $2^2 = 4$.

criteria.text: Substitutes correctly into ½mv² for the car at 13 m/s
Shows the energy is 4 times as much, not twice
Explains that it is 4 times because the speed is squared

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 1200 \times 169 = 101\,400$ J.

(b) At 26 m/s, $E_k = 600 \times 676 = 405\,600$ J, which is 4 times 101 400. So the claim is wrong: the energy is multiplied by 4, not 2, because the speed is squared in the formula and $2^2 = 4$.

questions.prompt:
To change a temperature in degrees Celsius, $C$, into degrees Fahrenheit, $F$, you can use $F = 1.8C + 32$.

(a) Change 25 °C into degrees Fahrenheit.

(b) A rule of thumb says *double the Celsius and add 30*. Compare the rule with the formula at 25 °C and at 0 °C.

(c) Find the Celsius temperature at which the rule of thumb gives exactly the right answer.
questions.solution:
(a) $F = 1.8 \times 25 + 32 = 45 + 32 = 77$ °F.

(b) At 25 °C the rule gives $2 \times 25 + 30 = 80$ °F, 3 degrees too high. At 0 °C it gives $30$ °F against the true $32$ °F, 2 degrees too low.

(c) The rule is exact where $2C + 30 = 1.8C + 32$. Subtract $1.8C$ and 30 from both sides: $0.2C = 2$, so $C = 10$. Check: both give 50 °F.

criteria.text: Finds the rule gives 80 °F at 25 °C, and says it is too high
Finds the rule gives 30 °F at 0 °C against 32 °F, and says it is too low
Sets the rule equal to the formula

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $1.8 \times 25 + 32 = 77$ °F.

(b) The rule gives 80 °F at 25 °C, 3 too many, and 30 °F at 0 °C, 2 too few, so it is close but not exact.

(c) $2C + 30 = 1.8C + 32$ gives $0.2C = 2$, so $C = 10$: at 10 °C both give 50 °F.

questions.prompt: Heron's formula gives the area of a triangle with sides $a$, $b$ and $c$ as $A = \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$, where $s = \dfrac{a + b + c}{2}$. Work out the area of a triangle with sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm.
questions.solution: First $s = \dfrac{13 + 14 + 15}{2} = 21$. Then $A = \sqrt{21 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6} = \sqrt{7056} = 84$ cm².

examTechnique.body:
**Write the formula out with the values in brackets before calculating anything.** It is the method mark, and it is where most errors are prevented.

**Do the powers first**, and remember a power belongs only to what it is written on.

**Type brackets into the calculator** round negative values, round the whole top and bottom of a fraction, and round everything under a root.

**If the unknown is not the subject, substitute and then solve.** Show the equation you get after substituting, because that line earns a method mark even if the algebra afterwards slips.

**Give units** when the question gives units, and round only at the end, to the accuracy asked for.
examinerErrors: Squaring the coefficient as well: working out $2x^2$ as $(2x)^2$.
Losing the sign when subtracting a negative: $4 - (-2)$ written as 2.
Dividing only the last term by the denominator of a fraction formula.
Rounding part-way through and giving a final answer that is out by the last digit.
Showing only the final answer, and so losing the method mark when it is wrong.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer writes every value into the formula in brackets before calculating, so the method is visible and the signs are safe. It squares only what the power is written on, reads fraction bars and roots as brackets, and keeps full calculator values until a single rounding at the end. When the unknown is not the subject it substitutes first and solves the equation that is left, checking by putting the answer back. Asked whether a claim is always true, it knows that one counterexample settles *no*, and that examples alone never settle *yes*.
